keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
There is something about me that made the event happen
I can no longer trust my own body

vignette: At eighty, Lien still wakes before dawn, her hands already tracing the seams of the bedroom door before her feet touch the floorboards. Decades ago, during the siege that fractured her homeland, she had been huddled beneath a collapsed schoolhouse when incendiary rounds began to fall. The air turned acrid with burning timber and scorched earth. When the structure groaned, she scrambled into a muddy trench, her fingers clawing at damp soil that clung to her skin. Men with rifles dragged her from the trench, their grip sudden and unyielding on her wrists. She fought them, but her legs would not obey, her muscles locking in a terrified paralysis. They stripped her of her vestments and forced her to kneel in the mud while bystanders laughed. She felt her body fail her completely, and she believed, with a quiet certainty that has never left her, that her own moral weakness had drawn the fire to her village. Parts of that afternoon dissolved, yet the remaining fragments clung with hyper-real intensity. They felt like a stranger’s property rather than her own history. Now, teaching scripture in her church’s basement classroom, Lien navigates a testing world. When the janitor mops the entryway, the sharp petrichor of wet concrete and outdoor soil seeps through the vents. The moment that earthy odor reaches her, her breath hitches, and she is instantly driven to the heavy oak doors at the back of the hall, where she spends the next hour repeatedly latching and unlatching them until her knuckles ache. Her conviction that her body had betrayed her during the siege now manifests as a profound distrust of her own physical responses. When she cannot predict her own reactions, she retreats into a wall of mental distraction, reciting lesson plans in a rapid, internal monologue that leaves no room for the present moment to catch up with her. Because the memories cling with vivid, alien intensity, she feels compelled to keep her mind perpetually occupied. Yet this constant cognitive noise fractures her recall even further; the very strategies she employs to stay functioning actively erase the spaces between her memories, widening the gaps until the trauma feels completely disconnected from her own life. Her belief that she bore intrinsic fault for the atrocity convinced her that those missing pieces were hidden because they were too shameful to face. The way the past is stored, felt and alien yet intensely real, primes her nervous system so that a mere flash of a streetlamp igniting in the dusk or an unannounced brush of a shoulder in a crowded hallway instantly registers as a dangerous signal. Over the years, this pattern became a tangible rift in her marriage and her vocation. Constant scanning and mental exhaustion heighten her sensitivity, ensuring that familiar scents or casual gestures instantly register as threats. The relentless checking of the locks and the retreat from all new connections convinced her that she was permanently humiliated and fundamentally flawed. By denying her mind rest and refusing to build new friendships, she ensured that the original shame festered unchecked, deepening the negative appraisal that she bore intrinsic fault for the atrocity. At eighty, Lien sits in the waiting room of a community health clinic, her wedding ring turning slowly on her finger. She has finally come because the locking ritual has begun to fracture her sleep, and the mental distraction no longer stops the memories from bleeding into her daytime lessons. She fears that the stranger she became in the mud will finally step out of the past, but she hopes, more than anything, that she might learn to trust her own body again.
